tips.title: Only one test needs heating
tips.body: **Benedict's** is the only one of the four that is **heated** — in a water bath, not over a flame. Iodine, Biuret and the ethanol emulsion are all done **cold**. A method that heats the Biuret test has described the wrong test.

tips.title: Give the colour before as well as after
tips.body: A positive result is a **change**, so name **both** colours: iodine **orange-brown to blue-black**, Biuret **blue to purple**. Giving both colours is safest, and shows you know what a negative looks like.

tips.title: Benedict's tells you how much, not just whether
tips.body: Benedict's goes **green → yellow → orange → brick red** as the concentration of reducing sugar rises. So it is **semi-quantitative**: a question giving four tubes of different colours is asking you to **rank** them, not just to say sugar is present.

tips.title: Ethanol first, then water
tips.body: The emulsion test is **ethanol, shake, then pour into water**. The cloudy white **emulsion** appears at the water step. Adding water first does nothing, because the fat has to dissolve in the ethanol before it can come out of solution.

tips.title: Calorimetry always underestimates
tips.body: Heat escapes to the air and to the apparatus, and the food rarely burns completely — so the measured energy is **always lower** than the true value. If a question asks why the answer is below the packet figure, that is the answer, and *every* improvement is about **reducing heat loss** or **burning the food fully**.

why.matters:
You cannot tell what is in a food by looking at it. Every one of these tests turns an invisible question — *is there protein in this?* — into a **colour change** you can see from across a bench, using a reagent chosen because its result is unmistakable.

Calorimetry does the same for energy. There is no instrument that reads joules out of a crisp, so the energy is moved somewhere it **can** be measured: into water, whose temperature rise can be measured.

examples.title: Four questions, four bottles
examples.body:
A food is mostly carbohydrate, protein and fat, and each has its own reagent. Iodine for starch, **Benedict's** for reducing sugars, the Biuret test (potassium hydroxide, then copper sulfate) for protein, and ethanol followed by water for fat.

Notice what they have in common: each gives a **change** rather than a state, which is why an answer has to name both colours. And only Benedict's is heated — the other three work cold, which is worth remembering because a question about the method is usually asking about exactly that.

visual.alt: A table of the four food tests: iodine for starch going orange-brown to blue-black, heated Benedict’s for reducing sugar going blue to brick red, Biuret for protein going blue to purple, and the ethanol emulsion test for fat

examples.title: Benedict's does not answer yes or no
examples.body:
Most tests are a yes or a no. Benedict's is different: the colour it ends up at depends on **how much** reducing sugar is there, running green, yellow, orange, brick red as the concentration rises.

That makes it **semi-quantitative** — a rough measurement rather than a detection. Before blood-glucose meters existed, that colour scale was how diabetes was monitored at home, and it is why a question can show you two tubes and ask which sample had more sugar in it.

visual.alt: A table of the Benedict’s colour scale: no reducing sugar leaves it blue, a little turns it green, more gives yellow to orange, and a lot gives a brick red precipitate

examples.title: Why the calorimetry answer is always too low
examples.body:
Burn a food under a boiling tube of water and the energy is whatever the water gained: 20 g warmed by 25 °C is **2100 J**, from temperature and mass alone.

It is also always an **underestimate**, and knowing why is most of the marks. Heat goes into the air, the glass and the apparatus rather than the water, and the food often does not burn completely. A result that came out **higher** than the label would not be a good experiment — it would be a mistake.

steps.title: Four foods, four reagents
steps.body:
This whole topic is **Biology only** (1.13B and 1.14B). The food tests are **core practical 1.13B**: using chemical reagents to identify **starch, reducing sugars, proteins and fats**.

Each test is a **reagent** and a **colour change**, and a question wants **both colours** — the one before and the one after — because that is what shows you could recognise a negative result too.

**Starch — iodine solution.** Add a few drops. **Orange-brown → blue-black.** No heating.

**Reducing sugars — Benedict's solution.** Add Benedict's and heat in a **water bath** at about **75 °C** for a few minutes. **Blue → green → yellow → orange → brick red**, and which one you get depends on **how much** sugar is there.

**Protein — the Biuret test.** Add **potassium hydroxide** solution to the food solution, then a few drops of **copper sulfate** solution, and mix. **Blue → purple** (sometimes described as lilac or mauve). **No heating.** Ready-mixed *Biuret solution* combines the two.

**Fats — the ethanol emulsion test.** Add **ethanol** and shake to dissolve any fat, then pour the liquid into **water**. A **cloudy white emulsion** means fat is present.

**The one that is different is Benedict's.** It is the only test that is **heated**, and the only one whose result tells you **how much** rather than simply **whether**.

steps.title: Benedict's, and reading how much
steps.body:
**Benedict's solution is blue to start with**, and stays blue if there is **no reducing sugar**. With sugar present, heating produces a **precipitate** whose colour depends on **how much sugar** there is:

- **green** — a trace
- **yellow** — a little more
- **orange** — more again
- **brick red** — the most

**So the test is semi-quantitative.** It does not give a number, but it **ranks** samples — and questions are set on exactly that. Four tubes showing blue, green, orange and brick red are four **concentrations**, in that order, and the answer is the ranking rather than *they all contain sugar*.

**Why a water bath rather than a Bunsen flame.** The tube is heated **evenly** and cannot be heated past **100 °C**, so the mixture does not spit or boil over. It is also the safer choice when flammable reagents are on the bench.

**What *reducing* means.** Not all sugars react: **glucose** and **fructose** do, and **sucrose** does not. You do not need to know why sucrose does not react, but you should expect a sucrose-only sample to stay blue.

**Two details that lose marks.** The solution must be **heated** — an unheated Benedict's test stays blue whatever is in it, so a student reporting *no sugar* after forgetting the water bath has produced a **false negative**. And the colour must be read **against the starting blue**, since a faint green is a positive result.

steps.title: The emulsion test, and doing the tests safely
steps.body:
**The ethanol emulsion test finds fats**, and the order of the steps is the whole method:

1. Add **ethanol** to the sample and **shake**. Fat **dissolves in ethanol**, though it does not dissolve in water.
2. **Pour the liquid into water.**
3. If fat is present it comes **out of solution** as tiny droplets, giving a **cloudy white emulsion**.

**The order matters and is examinable.** Adding **water first** does nothing, because the fat never dissolved — there is nothing to come out of solution. So a method that reverses the two steps produces a **false negative**.

**Preparing the food.** Solid food has to be **ground up** with a pestle and mortar and mixed with **distilled water**, then **filtered**, so that the reagents can reach the molecules. Distilled water is used so nothing dissolved in tap water affects the result. The **emulsion test** is the exception: it is done on a **fresh sample** of the food shaken with **ethanol**, not on the filtered water extract, because the fat has to dissolve in ethanol first and filtering can remove fat along with the solids.

**Testing one sample for several foods.** Take **separate portions** of the same solution into **separate tubes**, one per test. Running two reagents into one tube makes the colours impossible to read.

**Safety, which carries marks of its own:**

- **Ethanol is flammable** — keep it away from flames, which is another reason for a **water bath**.
- **Eye protection** throughout, because the Biuret test uses **potassium hydroxide**, which is corrosive.
- Handle hot tubes with **tongs**, and point them **away from people**.

steps.title: Calorimetry: measuring the energy in food
steps.body:
**Spec point 1.14B** asks how the energy in food can be measured. The idea is simple: **burn the food and use it to heat water**, then work out how much energy the water gained.

**The method:**

1. Measure a known **volume of water** into a boiling tube — $1\text{ cm}^3$ of water has a mass of **1 g**.
2. Record the **starting temperature**.
3. **Weigh** the food.
4. Set the food alight and hold it **under the tube** until it stops burning.
5. Record the **highest temperature** the water reaches.

$$\text{energy (J)} = \text{mass of water (g)} \times 4.2 \times \text{temperature rise (°C)}$$

Then divide by the **mass of the food** to get the energy **per gram**, which is what lets different foods be compared fairly.

equations.name: energy per gram = energy ÷ mass of food

steps.title: Why the answer always comes out too low
steps.body:
**A calorimetry result is always an underestimate**, and being able to say why — and what to do about it — is where the marks are.

**Where the energy goes instead of into the water:**

- **Heat lost to the surrounding air** as the food burns and as the tube stands in the open
- **Heat absorbed by the boiling tube itself**, and by the mounted needle and the stand
- **Incomplete combustion** — the food does not burn fully, so some of its energy is never released at all
- **Some food may not burn**, leaving a charred lump

**Every improvement follows from that list**, which is why the list is worth learning as a list:

- **Insulate** the boiling tube, or use a **draught shield**, to cut heat loss to the air
- **Hold the food closer** to the tube, so less heat escapes on the way
- **Relight** the food if it goes out, so combustion is more complete
- **Burn it in oxygen** rather than air, as a real bomb calorimeter does
- **Stir** the water, so the thermometer reads the true average temperature

**Note which way the error runs.** Every one of these losses makes the measured energy **lower** than the true value — none of them makes it higher. So if a question says the packet claims more energy than the experiment found, you do **not** need to suggest the packet is wrong: the experiment is **expected** to read low.

**A bomb calorimeter** is the industrial version: the food is burned in **pure oxygen** inside a sealed, **insulated** container surrounded by water. It fixes all four problems at once, so it gives values much closer to the true energy content.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Give both colours, always.** A positive result is a **change**, so *orange-brown to blue-black* is the answer and *turns blue-black* is half of it. The same applies to Biuret: **blue to purple**. The second colour on its own does not show that you would recognise a negative.

**Benedict's measures amount, not just presence.** The scale **blue → green → yellow → orange → brick red** is the reason the test is called **semi-quantitative**, and a question with several tubes is asking you to **rank concentrations**. Answering *they all contain sugar* throws away the whole point of the test — and the blue tube does not contain any.

**A false negative is a specific, examinable idea.** Two of these tests produce one if the method is wrong: an **unheated** Benedict's tube **stays blue** whatever is in it, and an emulsion test done **water first** stays clear because the fat never dissolved. Being able to say *that is a false negative, and here is the step that caused it* is a strong answer.

**The calorimetry error runs one way, and knowing that settles the question.** Heat lost to the air, heat taken by the tube, and **incomplete combustion** all mean **less** energy reaches the water — so the measured value is **always an underestimate**. You never need to argue that the packet is wrong. And every improvement worth naming reduces **heat loss** or improves **combustion**; that is the pattern, rather than five unrelated facts.

**Divide by the mass of the food, not the water.** The equation uses the **water's** mass to find the joules; the **per-gram** step uses the **food's** mass. Mixing those up is the commonest calculation error here, and it is worth a quick check: dividing by a mass below 1 g must make the number **bigger**.

**And per gram is what makes a comparison fair.** Two foods burned in different amounts cannot be compared by raw joules. Converting both to **J/g** can reverse the apparent order — as it does in the two worked examples — which is exactly why the spec asks for it.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- This topic is **Biology only** (1.13B and 1.14B), and the tests are **core practical 1.13B**.
- **Starch**: **iodine**, **orange-brown → blue-black**. Not heated.
- **Reducing sugar**: **Benedict's**, heated in a **water bath**; **blue → green → yellow → orange → brick red**.
- **Protein**: the **Biuret test**, **potassium hydroxide** then **copper sulfate**; **blue → purple**. Not heated.
- **Fat**: **ethanol**, shake, then pour into **water**; a **cloudy white emulsion**.
- **Benedict's is the only test that is heated**, and the only one that shows **how much** — it is **semi-quantitative**.
- An **unheated** Benedict's test stays blue: a **false negative**.
- The emulsion test is **ethanol first, water second**. Reversed, it gives a **false negative**.
- Prepare food by **grinding** with **distilled water** and **filtering**, and use a **separate portion** for each test; the emulsion test uses a **fresh sample** shaken with **ethanol**.
- Safety: **ethanol is flammable**; the Biuret test uses **potassium hydroxide**, which is corrosive, so wear **eye protection**.
- **Calorimetry**: burn a weighed food sample under a known volume of water and record the **temperature rise**.
- $\text{energy (J)} = \text{mass of water (g)} \times 4.2 \times \text{temperature rise}$; $1\text{ cm}^3$ of water is **1 g**.
- **Energy per gram = energy ÷ mass of the food**, and that is what makes two foods comparable.
- The result is **always an underestimate**: **heat lost** to the air and the apparatus, and **incomplete combustion**.
- Improvements all reduce **heat loss** or improve **combustion**: insulate, use a draught shield, hold the food closer, relight it, stir the water.
- A **bomb calorimeter** burns the food in **pure oxygen** in a sealed insulated container, so its values are much closer to the true energy content.

questions.prompt: A student is given an unknown food. Describe how they would test it for starch, reducing sugars, protein and fat, giving the reagent and the colour change for each, and explain two ways their method could produce a false negative.
questions.solution:
I would grind the food with **distilled water**, filter it, and take a **separate portion** of the solution for each of the starch, protein and sugar tests, because running two reagents into one tube makes the colours impossible to read.

For **starch**, add a few drops of **iodine solution**. It is **orange-brown** to begin with and turns **blue-black** if starch is present. No heating is needed.

For **protein**, use the **Biuret test**: add **potassium hydroxide** solution, then a few drops of **copper sulfate** solution. The mixture is **blue** and turns **purple** if protein is present. Again no heating — and eye protection matters here, because **potassium hydroxide** is corrosive.

For **reducing sugars**, add **Benedict's solution** and heat the tube in a **water bath** at about 75 °C for a few minutes. It stays **blue** if there is none, and turns **green, yellow, orange or brick red** depending on **how much** sugar is present — so this test also ranks concentrations rather than simply detecting.

For **fat**, I would use a **fresh sample** of the food rather than the water extract: shake it with **ethanol** so that any fat **dissolves**, then pour the liquid into **water**. A **cloudy white emulsion** shows fat is present.

Two steps in that method, done wrongly, produce a **false negative** — a result that looks negative but was caused by the procedure rather than the sample. First, if the **Benedict's test is not heated**, the tube **stays blue whatever is in it**, and a student would wrongly record that there is no sugar. Second, if **water is added before the ethanol** in the emulsion test, the fat **never dissolves**, so there is nothing to come out of solution and the tube stays clear — again suggesting, wrongly, that there is no fat. questions.modelAnswer:
I would grind the food with **distilled water**, filter it, and take a **separate portion** of the solution for each of the starch, protein and sugar tests, because running two reagents into one tube makes the colours impossible to read.

For **starch**, add a few drops of **iodine solution**. It is **orange-brown** to begin with and turns **blue-black** if starch is present. No heating is needed.

For **protein**, use the **Biuret test**: add **potassium hydroxide** solution, then a few drops of **copper sulfate** solution. The mixture is **blue** and turns **purple** if protein is present. Again no heating — and eye protection matters here, because **potassium hydroxide** is corrosive.

For **reducing sugars**, add **Benedict's solution** and heat the tube in a **water bath** at about 75 °C for a few minutes. It stays **blue** if there is none, and turns **green, yellow, orange or brick red** depending on **how much** sugar is present — so this test also ranks concentrations rather than simply detecting.

For **fat**, I would use a **fresh sample** of the food rather than the water extract: shake it with **ethanol** so that any fat **dissolves**, then pour the liquid into **water**. A **cloudy white emulsion** shows fat is present.

Two steps in that method, done wrongly, produce a **false negative** — a result that looks negative but was caused by the procedure rather than the sample. First, if the **Benedict's test is not heated**, the tube **stays blue whatever is in it**, and a student would wrongly record that there is no sugar. Second, if **water is added before the ethanol** in the emulsion test, the fat **never dissolves**, so there is nothing to come out of solution and the tube stays clear — again suggesting, wrongly, that there is no fat. In both cases the sample is fine and the method is at fault, which is why the order and the heating are part of the test rather than details.

questions.prompt: A student burns 0.6 g of a crisp under 20 cm³ of water and records a temperature rise of 25 °C. Calculate the energy per gram, and evaluate how reliable this value is compared with the figure printed on the packet.
questions.solution:
The water has a mass of **20 g**, because $1\text{ cm}^3$ of water has a mass of 1 g. The energy transferred to it is $20 \times 4.2 \times 25 = \textbf{2100 J}$. Dividing by the mass of the **food** — not the water — gives $\dfrac{2100}{0.6} = \textbf{3500 J/g}$.

That value will be **lower than the true energy content**, and it is worth being clear that the error runs only one way. Heat is **lost to the surrounding air** while the crisp burns and while the tube stands open. More heat is **absorbed by the boiling tube itself** and by the stand rather than by the water. And the crisp almost certainly does **not burn completely** — a charred fragment is usually left, and the energy still locked in it is never released. Every one of these makes the measured value **smaller**. None of them could make it larger.

That matters for the comparison. If the packet claims more energy per gram than 3500 J/g, the student does **not** need to suspect the packet: their experiment is **expected** to read low. A result **higher** than the packet would be the surprising one.

The method can be improved, and every worthwhile improvement targets one of the two causes. To cut **heat loss**: **insulate** the boiling tube, put a **draught shield** around the apparatus, and hold the burning food **closer** to the tube so less heat escapes on the way. To improve **combustion**: **relight** the food if it goes out, so more of it burns. **Stirring** the water before reading the thermometer also helps, since otherwise the reading is of one spot rather than the average.

The industrial answer to all of this is a **bomb calorimeter**, which burns the food in **pure oxygen** inside a **sealed, insulated** container surrounded by water. Complete combustion and almost no heat loss are exactly the two problems the school method cannot solve, which is why a bomb calorimeter gives values much closer to the true energy content, and higher than anything a boiling tube will give.

questions.prompt: In the Biuret test for protein, which reagents are added to the food solution, and in what order?
questions.solution: **Potassium hydroxide, then copper sulfate.** A purple colour shows protein; if it stays blue there is none. No heating is needed, and eye protection is worn because potassium hydroxide is corrosive.

examTechnique.body:
Two different skills are examined here. The **food tests** are recall, but recall of a **change**: name the reagent, the colour **before** and the colour **after**. Giving both colours is safest, and shows you know what a negative looks like.

The **calorimetry** half is a calculation followed by an **evaluation**, and the evaluation is worth as much as the arithmetic. Learn the errors as a short list with the improvement attached to each, because the question almost always asks for both.
examinerErrors: Giving only the **final** colour, rather than the change — *orange-brown to blue-black*.
Forgetting that **Benedict's must be heated**, and so describing a test that would stay blue whatever the sample.
Doing the emulsion test **water first**, which dissolves nothing and gives a **false negative**.
Treating **Benedict's** as a yes-or-no test when the colour shows **how much**.
Using the mass of the **water** in the per-gram step instead of the mass of the **food**.
Forgetting that $1\text{ cm}^3$ of water has a mass of **1 g**, and so having no mass to put in the equation.
Suggesting the **packet is wrong** when the experiment reads low, rather than **heat loss** and **incomplete combustion**.
Offering improvements that raise **precision**, such as a better balance, when the problem is a **systematic** heat loss.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer treats a **false negative** as a named idea rather than a mistake: it can point at the step — the unheated tube, or the water poured in first — and say why the result looks negative when the sample is not. It reads **Benedict's** as a **scale**, ranking tubes by concentration rather than reporting that sugar is present. In calorimetry it divides by the mass of the **food**, notices that dividing by less than a gram must make the number **bigger**, and states that every source of error pushes the value **down**, so the experiment is expected to underestimate and the packet needs no defending. Asked to improve the method, it matches each improvement to the loss it fixes, and finishes with the **bomb calorimeter**, which fixes both at once.
